current_example.title: Example: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient

q-37341.name: Question 1
q-37341.problem: Evaluate the gradient of $g(x,y)$ at the point $({e}^{2},1)$ if $g(x,y)=(x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}).$
q-37341.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =1\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})+(x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}+1+\frac{y}{x} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =1\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})+(x+y)\cdot (-2y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}-2xy-2{y}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-3{y}^{2}-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),\,{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}+1+\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x-3{y}^{2}-2xy⟩ \\ ∇g({e}^{2},1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-{1}^{2}+1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-3\cdot {1}^{2}-2\cdot {e}^{2}\cdot 1⟩ \\  & =⟨2+{e}^{-2},-1-2{e}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

q-37341.html:
Question 1
?

Evaluate the gradient of g(x,y) at the point (e2,1) if g(x,y)=(x+y)(ln⁡x−y2).

a
 ⟨e−2,1−2e2⟩
b
 ⟨2+e−2,−1−2e2⟩
c
 ⟨2+e−2,2e2⟩
d
 ⟨2+e2,1+2e2⟩
e
 ⟨2+e2,−1−2e−2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives gx(x,y)=∂∂x((x+y)(ln⁡x−y2))=1⋅(ln⁡x−y2)+(x+y)⋅1x=ln⁡x−y2+1+yxgy(x,y)=∂∂y((x+y)(ln⁡x−y2))=1⋅(ln⁡x−y2)+(x+y)⋅(−2y)=ln⁡x−y2−2xy−2y2=ln⁡x−3y2−2xy

Hence, the gradient is ∇g(x,y)=⟨gx(x,y),gy(x,y)⟩=⟨ln⁡x−y2+1+yx,ln⁡x−3y2−2xy⟩∇g(e2,1)=⟨ln⁡(e2)−12+1+1e2,ln⁡(e2)−3⋅12−2⋅e2⋅1⟩=⟨2+e−2,−1−2e2⟩

q-127649.name: Question 2
q-127649.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x}{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{y}){e}^{x/y} \\  & =\frac{x-y}{{x}^{2}}{e}^{x/y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x}{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{y}{x}\cdot \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}){e}^{x/y} \\  & =\frac{y-x}{xy}{e}^{x/y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{x-y}{{x}^{2}}{e}^{x/y}\text{ }i+\frac{y-x}{xy}{e}^{x/y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=yxex/y, find ∇f(x,y).

a
 x2−y2x2ex/yi+y2−x2xyex/yj
b
 x−yx2ex/yi+y−xxyex/yj
c
 1−y2x2yex/yi+x2−1xy2ex/yj
d
−yx2ex/yi+xy2ex/yj
e
1−yx2yex/yi+x−1xy2ex/yj
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: fx(x,y)=∂∂x(yxex/y)=(−yx2+yx⋅1y)ex/y=x−yx2ex/yfy(x,y)=∂∂y(yxex/y)=(1x−yx⋅xy2)ex/y=y−xxyex/y

Hence, the gradient is ∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y) i+fy(x,y) j=x−yx2ex/y i+y−xxyex/y j.

q-35988.name: Question 3
q-35988.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{3x+2y}{x-y}) \\  & =\frac{3(x-y)-(3x+2y)}{(x-y)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5y}{(x-y)^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{3x+2y}{x-y}) \\  & =\frac{2(x-y)+(3x+2y)}{(x-y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5x}{(x-y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =-\frac{5y}{(x-y)^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{5x}{(x-y)^{2}}\text{ }j \\  & =-\frac{5}{(x-y)^{2}}\text{ }(y\text{ }i-x\text{ }j)\end{aligned}
$$

q-35988.html:
Question 3
?

Given f(x,y)=3x+2yx−y, find ∇f(x,y).

a
 −5 (x i−y j)
b
 −5(x−y)2 (x i−y j)
c
 5(x−y)2 (y i+x j)
d
 −5 (y i−x j)
e
 −5(x−y)2 (y i−x j)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: fx(x,y)=∂∂x(3x+2yx−y)=3(x−y)−(3x+2y)(x−y)2=−5y(x−y)2fy(x,y)=∂∂y(3x+2yx−y)=2(x−y)+(3x+2y)(x−y)2=5x(x−y)2

Hence, the gradient is:

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y) i+fy(x,y) j=−5y(x−y)2 i+5x(x−y)2 j=−5(x−y)2 (y i−x j)
q-35988.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables

q-36909.name: Question 4
q-36909.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =2x\sqrt{y+3} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),\,{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\sqrt{y+3},\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}⟩ \\ ∇f(2,1) & =⟨2\cdot 2\sqrt{1+3},\,\frac{{2}^{2}}{2\sqrt{1+3}}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

q-36909.html:
Question 4
?

Evaluate ∇f(x,y) at (2,1) if f(x,y)=x2y+3.

a
 ⟨16,1⟩
b
 ⟨2,0⟩
c
 ⟨8,1⟩
d
 ⟨1,8⟩
e
 ⟨4,12⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

fx(x,y)=∂∂x(x2y+3)=2xy+3fy(x,y)=∂∂y(x2y+3)=x22y+3. Hence, the gradient is:

∇f(x,y)=⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨2xy+3,x22y+3⟩∇f(2,1)=⟨2⋅21+3,2221+3⟩=⟨8,1⟩
q-36909.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables

q-36005.name: Question 5
q-36005.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =⟨{h}_{x}(x,y),\,{h}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y,\,\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}⟩ \\ ∇h(1,1) & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡1,\,\frac{4\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{4}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36005.html:
Question 5
?

Evaluate ∇h(x,y) at (1,1) if h(x,y)=4xarctan⁡y.

a
 ⟨π,2⟩
b
 ⟨π,12⟩
c
 ⟨π4,12⟩
d
 ⟨1,1⟩
e
 ⟨2π,0⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives hx(x,y)=∂∂x(4xarctan⁡y)=4arctan⁡yhy(x,y)=∂∂y(4xarctan⁡y)=4xy2+1 Hence, the gradient is ∇h(x,y)=⟨hx(x,y),hy(x,y)⟩=⟨4arctan⁡y,4xy2+1⟩∇h(1,1)=⟨4arctan⁡1,4⋅112+1⟩=⟨4⋅π4,42⟩=⟨π,2⟩.
q-36005.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables

q-35989.name: Question 6
q-35989.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2z{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1) \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2y{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1) \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2x{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =2z{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }i+2y{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+2x{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }k \\  & =2{e}^{2xz}\text{ }(z\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)i+y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+x\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }k)\end{aligned}
$$

q-35989.html:
Question 6
?

Given g(x,y,z)=e2xzsin⁡(y2−1), find ∇g(x,y,z).

a
 2e2xz (zi+y j+x k)
b
 2e2xz (zi+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+x k)
c
 2e2xz (zsin⁡(y2−1)i+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+xsin⁡(y2−1) k)
d
 zsin⁡(y2−1)i+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+xsin⁡(y2−1) k
e
 2e2xzsin⁡(y2−1) (zi+y j+x k)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

gx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(e2xzsin⁡(y2−1))=2ze2xzsin⁡(y2−1)gy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(e2xzsin⁡(y2−1))=2ye2xzcos⁡(y2−1)gz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(e2xzsin⁡(y2−1))=2xe2xzsin⁡(y2−1).

Hence, the gradient is: ∇g(x,y,z)=gx(x,y,z) i+gy(x,y,z) j+gz(x,y,z) k=2ze2xzsin⁡(y2−1) i+2ye2xzcos⁡(y2−1) j+2xe2xzsin⁡(y2−1) k=2e2xz (zsin⁡(y2−1)i+ycos⁡(y2−1) j+xsin⁡(y2−1) k)

q-127950.html:
Question 7
?

Find ∇f(x,y,z), given that f(x,y,z)=1(x2+y2+z2)1/2.

a
 −1(x2+y2+z2)1/2(x2i+y2j+z2k)
b
1(x2+y2+z2)1/2(xi+yj+zk)
c
 1(x2+y2+z2)3/2(x2i+y2j+z2k)
d
2(x2+y2+z2)3/2(xi+yj+zk)
e
−1(x2+y2+z2)3/2(xi+yj+zk)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

fx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(1x2+y2+z2)=−x(x2+y2+z2)3/2fy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(1x2+y2+z2)=−y(x2+y2+z2)3/2fz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(1x2+y2+z2)=−z(x2+y2+z2)3/2.

Hence, the gradient is ∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z) i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=(−x(x2+y2+z2)3/2)i+(−y(x2+y2+z2)3/2)j+(−z(x2+y2+z2)3/2)k=−1(x2+y2+z2)3/2(xi+yj+zk)
q-127950.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables

q-127945.name: Question 8
q-127945.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & =y{x}^{y-1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,i+({x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1})j+{y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

q-127945.html:
Question 8
?

If f(x,y,z)=xy+yz, find ∇f(x,y,z).

a
yxy−1i+zyz−1j+yzln⁡yk
b
(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)i+xyln⁡yj+yzln⁡zk
c
xyln⁡yi+xyln⁡xj+(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)k
d
yxy−1i+zyz−1j+zyz−1k
e
 yxy−1i+(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)j+yzln⁡yk
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: fx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(xy+yz)=yxy−1fy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(xy+yz)=xyln⁡x+zyz−1fz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(xy+yz)=yzln⁡y

Hence, the gradient is ∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=yxy−1i+(xyln⁡x+zyz−1)j+yzln⁡yk.
q-127945.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables

q-36968.name: Question 9
q-36968.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x+2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{yz})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+2}}+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+2}} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{yz})) \\  & =0+\frac{1}{\sqrt{yz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{yz}}\cdot z \\  & =\frac{1}{2y} \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x+2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{yz})) \\  & =0+\frac{1}{\sqrt{yz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{yz}}\cdot y \\  & =\frac{1}{2z}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,  the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+2}}i+\frac{1}{2y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{2z}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

q-36968.html:
Question 9
?

Find ∇g(x,y,z) given that g(x,y,z)=x+2+ln⁡(yz).

a
 12x+2i+12y j+12z k
b
 12x+2i+12yz j+12yz k
c
 12x+2i+12y j+12z k
d
 1x+2i+1yz j+1yz k
e
 1x+2i+1y j+1z k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: gx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(x+2+ln⁡(yz))=12x+2+0=12x+2gy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(x+2+ln⁡(yz))=0+1yz⋅12yz⋅z=12ygz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(x+2+ln⁡(yz))=0+1yz⋅12yz⋅y=12z

Hence, the gradient is: ∇g(x,y,z)=gx(x,y,z) i+gy(x,y,z) j+gz(x,y,z) k=12x+2i+12y j+12z k
q-36968.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables

q-71425.name: Question 10
q-71425.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+yz{e}^{xyz} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2{x}^{2}y{z}^{2}+xz{e}^{xyz} \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+xy{e}^{xyz}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,  the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+yz{e}^{xyz})\text{ }i+(2{x}^{2}y{z}^{2}+xz{e}^{xyz})\text{ }j+(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+xy{e}^{xyz})\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

q-71425.html:
Question 10
?

Find ∇g(x,y,z) given that g(x,y,z)=x2y2z2+exyz.

a
(2xy2z2+exyz) i+(2x2yz2+exyz) j+(2x2y2z+exyz) k
b
(2xy2z2+yzexyz) i+(2x2yz2+xzexyz) j+(2x2y2z+xyexyz) k
c
(2x+yzexyz) i+(2y+xzexyz) j+(2z+xyexyz) k
d
(xy2z2+yzexyz−1) i+(x2yz2+xzexyz−1) j+(x2y2z+xyexyz−1) k
e
(2xy2z2+xexyz) i+(2x2yz2+yexyz) j+(2x2y2z+zexyz) k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives: gx(x,y,z)=∂∂x(x2y2z2+exyz)=2xy2z2+yzexyzgy(x,y,z)=∂∂y(x2y2z2+exyz)=2x2yz2+xzexyzgz(x,y,z)=∂∂z(x2y2z2+exyz)=2x2y2z+xyexyz

Hence, the gradient is: ∇g(x,y,z)=gx(x,y,z) i+gy(x,y,z) j+gz(x,y,z) k=(2xy2z2+yzexyz) i+(2x2yz2+xzexyz) j+(2x2y2z+xyexyz) k

q-128517.name: Question 11
q-128517.problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ find the points $(x,y),$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$
q-128517.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0 \\ 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2y & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=0,$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$

- For $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0,$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ at two points: $(1,0)$ and $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

q-128518.name: Question 12
q-128518.problem: Given that $h(x,y)=({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇h(x,y)=0.$
q-128518.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}) \\  & =2x{e}^{x}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}) \\  & =-2y{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y)=({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}\,i-2y{e}^{x}\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇h(x,y)=0:$

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}\,i-2y{e}^{x}\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}=0, \\ -2y{e}^{x}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+2x-{0}^{2}){e}^{x} & =0 \\ x(x+2){e}^{x} & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0$ at two points: $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0).$

?

a
 (0,0) and (2,0)
b
(2,0) only
c
(0,0) only
d
 (−2,0) only

 (−2,0) and (0,0)

∂h∂x=∂∂x((x2−y2)ex)=2xex+(x2−y2)ex=(x2+2x−y2)ex∂h∂y=∂∂y((x2−y2)ex)=−2yex

Hence, ∇h(x,y)=(x2+2x−y2)exi−2yexj.

Now, we solve ∇h(x,y)=0:

(x2+2x−y2)exi−2yexj=0 i+0 j

So, by equating the coefficients of i and j, we obtain

{(x2+2x−y2)ex=0,−2yex=0. From the second equation, we get y=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain (x2+2x−02)ex=0x(x+2)ex=0x=−2,0.

Therefore, ∇h(x,y)=0 at two points: (−2,0) and (0,0).

q-71437.name: Question 13
q-71437.problem: Given that $g(x,y)=4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇g(x,y)=0.$
q-71437.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4y+0-2x \\  & =2(2y-x) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x+2y-0 \\  & =2(2x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y)=2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y)=0:$

$$
2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2y-x=0 \\ 2x+y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=2y.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2y)+y & =0 \\ 5y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get $x=2\cdot 0=0.$

Therefore, $∇g(x,y)=0$ at the point $(0,0).$

q-71437.html:
Question 13
?

Given that g(x,y)=4xy+y2−x2, find the points (x,y) where ∇g(x,y)=0.

a
(0,0)
b
(−2,−1)
c
(2,1)
d
(4,−2)
e
(4,2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂g∂x=∂∂x(4xy+y2−x2)=4y+0−2x=2(2y−x)∂g∂y=∂∂y(4xy+y2−x2)=4x+2y−0=2(2x+y)

Hence, ∇g(x,y)=2(2y−x)i+2(2x+y)j.

Now, we solve ∇g(x,y)=0:

2(2y−x)i+2(2x+y)j=0 i+0 j

So, by equating the coefficients of i and j, we obtain:

{2y−x=02x+y=0 From the first equation, we get x=2y. Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain: 2(2y)+y=05y=0y=0

Finally, we get x=2⋅0=0.

Therefore, ∇g(x,y)=0 at the point (0,0).

q-71475.name: Question 14
q-71475.problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇g(x,y,z)=0.$
q-71475.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+0+0-1-0-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{1}{y}+0-0-1-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+0+\operatorname{ln}⁡z+z\cdot \frac{1}{z}-0-0-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=1.$  Similarly, from the second and third equations, we obtain $y=1$ and $z=1.$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=0$ at the point $(1,1,1).$

q-71475.html:
Question 14
?

Given that g(x,y,z)=xln⁡x+yln⁡y+zln⁡z−x−y−z, find the points (x,y,z) where ∇g(x,y,z)=0.

a
(−1,−1,−1)
b
(0,0,0)
c
(1,1,1)
d
(1e,1e,1e)
e
(e,e,e)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂g∂x=∂∂x(xln⁡x+yln⁡y+zln⁡z−x−y−z)=ln⁡x+x⋅1x+0+0−1−0−0=ln⁡x+1−1=ln⁡x∂g∂y=∂∂y(xln⁡x+yln⁡y+zln⁡z−x−y−z)=0+ln⁡y+y⋅1y+0−0−1−0=ln⁡y+1−1=ln⁡y∂g∂z=∂∂z(xln⁡x+yln⁡y+zln⁡z−x−y−z)=0+0+ln⁡z+z⋅1z−0−0−1=ln⁡z+1−1=ln⁡z

Hence, ∇g(x,y,z)=ln⁡xi+ln⁡yj+ln⁡zk.

Now, we solve ∇g(x,y,z)=0:

ln⁡xi+ln⁡yj+ln⁡zk=0 i+0 j+0 j

So, by equating the coefficient of i, j, and k, we obtain: {ln⁡x=0ln⁡y=0ln⁡z=0

From the first equation, we get x=1. Similarly, from the second and third equations, we obtain y=1 and z=1.

Hence, ∇g(x,y,z)=0 at the point (1,1,1).

q-71474.name: Question 15
q-71474.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇f(x,y,z)=0.$
q-71474.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}+0-\frac{1}{z{x}^{2}}-0 \\  & =-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}+0-0 \\  & =-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =0+0-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}x}-1 \\  & =-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}=0 \\ -\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=-1.$ Substituting these into the third equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x} & =0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}(-1)}{{z}^{2}(-1)} & =0 \\ 1-{z}^{2} & =0 \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{(-1)^{2}yz} & =0 \\ z+y & =0 \\ y & =-z\end{aligned}
$$

When $z=1,$ we have $y=-1$ and when $z=-1,$ we have $y=1.$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(-1,1,-1).$

q-71474.html:
Question 15
?

Given that f(x,y,z)=1xy+1y+1zx−z, find the points (x,y,z) where ∇f(x,y,z)=0.

a
(−1,−1,−1) and (−1,1,1)
b
(−1,1,−1) only
c
(1,−1,−1) and (1,1,1)
d
(−1,−1,1) only
e
(−1,−1,1) and (−1,1,−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂f∂x=∂∂x(1xy+1y+1zx−z)=−1x2y+0−1zx2−0=−z+yx2yz∂f∂y=∂∂y(1xy+1y+1zx−z)=−1xy2−1y2+0−0=−1+xxy2∂f∂z=∂∂z(1xy+1y+1zx−z)=0+0−1z2x−1=−1+z2xz2x

Hence, ∇f(x,y,z)=−z+yx2yzi−1+xxy2j−1+z2xz2xk.

Now, we solve ∇f(x,y,z)=0:

−z+yx2yzi−1+xxy2j−1+z2xz2xk=0 i+0 j+0 j

So, by equating the coefficient of i, j, and k, we obtain: {−z+yx2yz=0−1+xxy2=0−1+z2xz2x=0

From the second equation, we get x=−1. Substituting these into the third equation, we obtain: −1+z2xz2x=0−1+z2(−1)z2(−1)=01−z2=0z2=1z=±1

Substituting x=−1 into the first equation, we obtain: −z+y(−1)2yz=0z+y=0y=−z

When z=1, we have y=−1 and when z=−1, we have y=1.

Hence, ∇f(x,y,z)=0 at two points: (−1,−1,1) and (−1,1,−1).

q-128528.name: Question 16
q-128528.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}),\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
q-128528.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j)+\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j) \\  & =\frac{y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i-\frac{x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j+\frac{x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j+\frac{x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{y+x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})-x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}((y+x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}))i+(y\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})-x)j).\end{aligned}
$$

q-128528.html:
Question 16
?

Find the gradient of the product f(x,y)h(x,y), given that f(x,y)=arctan⁡(xy),∇f(x,y)=yx2+y2i−xx2+y2j,h(x,y)=x2+y2,∇h(x,y)=xx2+y2i+yx2+y2j.

a
1x2+y2((y−xarctan⁡(xy))i+(x+yarctan⁡(xy))j)
b
x2+y2((y−xarctan⁡(xy))i+(x+yarctan⁡(xy))j)
c
x2+y2((x−yarctan⁡(xy))i+(y−xarctan⁡(xy))j)
d
1x2+y2((y+xarctan⁡(xy))i+(yarctan⁡(xy)−x)j)
e
1x2+y2((x−yarctan⁡(xy))i+(y−xarctan⁡(xy))j)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by ∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.

Using the product rule, we obtain ∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)]=h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y)=x2+y2(yx2+y2i−xx2+y2j)+arctan⁡(xy)(xx2+y2i+yx2+y2j)=yx2+y2x2+y2i−xx2+y2x2+y2j+xarctan⁡(xy)x2+y2i+yarctan⁡(xy)x2+y2j=yx2+y2i−xx2+y2j+xarctan⁡(xy)x2+y2i+yarctan⁡(xy)x2+y2j=y+xarctan⁡(xy)x2+y2i+yarctan⁡(xy)−xx2+y2j=1x2+y2((y+xarctan⁡(xy))i+(yarctan⁡(xy)−x)j).

q-65135.name: Question 17
q-65135.problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y)$ if $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$ and $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}?$
q-65135.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=f\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,f
$$

First, we calculate the first order partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j={e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\text{ }j=2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =({e}^{x+y})(2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})({e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =2x{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+2y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2y+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

q-65135.html:
Question 17
?

What is the gradient of the product f(x,y)g(x,y) if f(x,y)=ex+y and g(x,y)=x2+y2?

a
(x2+2x)ex+y i+(x2+2y)ex+y j
b
(x+2x2)ex+y i+(x+2y2)ex+y j
c
(x2+2x+y2)ex+y i+(x2+2y+y2)ex+y j
d
(x+y)2ex+y i+(x2+y)2ex+y j
e
x2ex+y i+y2ex+y j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and g(x,y) is given by:

∇[fg]=f∇g+g∇f

First, we calculate the first order partial derivatives of f(x,y):

∂f∂x=∂∂x(ex+y)=ex+y∂f∂y=∂∂y(ex+y)=ex+y

Hence, ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂x i+∂f∂y j=ex+y i+ex+y j.

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(x2+y2)=2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(x2+y2)=2y

Therefore, ∇g(x,y)=∂g∂x i+∂g∂y j=2x i+2y j.

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)]=(ex+y)(2x i+2y j)+(x2+y2)(ex+y i+ex+y j)=2xex+y i+2yex+y j+(x2+y2)ex+y i+(x2+y2)ex+y j=(x2+2x+y2)ex+y i+(x2+2y+y2)ex+y j

q-71476.name: Question 18
q-71476.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2},\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=(2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\frac{1}{xy},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
q-71476.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=h\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}((2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2xy+{y}^{2}}{xy}\text{ }i+\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2x+y}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{x+2y}{y}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{x+y}{x}\text{ }i-\frac{x+y}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =(-\frac{x+y}{x}+\frac{2x+y}{x})\text{ }i+(-\frac{x+y}{y}+\frac{x+2y}{y})\text{ }j \\  & =\text{ }i+\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Find the gradient of the product f(x,y)h(x,y), given that f(x,y)=x2y+xy2,∇f(x,y)=(2xy+y2) i+(x2+2xy) j,h(x,y)=1xy,∇h(x,y)=−1x2y i−1xy2 j.

a
 i+ j
b
y i+x j
c
 i− j
d
x i+y j
e
− i+ j
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by:

∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h

Using the product rule, we obtain:

∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)]=h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y)=1xy((2xy+y2) i+(x2+2xy) j)+(x2y+xy2)(−1x2y i−1xy2 j)=(2xy+y2xy i+x2+2xyxy j)+(−x2y+xy2x2y i−x2y+xy2xy2 j)=(2x+yx i+x+2yy j)+(−x+yx i−x+yy j)=(−x+yx+2x+yx) i+(−x+yy+x+2yy) j= i+ j
q-71476.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient

q-71477.name: Question 19
q-71477.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =x+y,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=\text{ }i+\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
q-71477.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)(\text{ }i+\text{ }j)+(x+y)(\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\text{ }i)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+1\text{ }j) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }i+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

q-128524.name: Question 20
q-128524.problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)?$
q-128524.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

q-128524.html:
Question 20
?

What is the gradient of the product f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z) if f(x,y,z)=xyz and h(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz)?

a
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(x2 i+y2 j+z2 k)
b
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(x i+y j+z k)
c
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(i+j+k)
d
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))((y+z) i+(x+z) j+(x+y) k)
e
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(yz i+xz j+xy k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by ∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of f(x,y,z):

∂f∂x=∂∂x(xyz)=yz∂f∂y=∂∂y(xyz)=xz∂f∂z=∂∂z(xyz)=xy

Hence, ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂x i+∂f∂y j+∂f∂z k=yz i+xz j+xy k.

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of h(x,y,z):

∂h∂x=∂∂x(ln⁡(xyz))=1x∂h∂y=∂∂y(ln⁡(xyz))=1y∂h∂z=∂∂z(ln⁡(xyz))=1z

Therefore, ∇h(x,y,z)=∂h∂x i+∂h∂y j+∂h∂z k=1x i+1y j+1z k.

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain ∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)]=f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)=xyz(1x i+1y j+1z k)+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=xyzx i+xyzy j+xyzz k+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=yz i+xz j+xy k+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=(1+ln⁡(xyz))(yz i+xz j+xy k).
